title: Latitude had a clear link to lilac spring sensitivity in one of four plant and year models for US records in 1965-2008
abstract: We tested whether first lilac bloom had a weaker response to spring warmth farther north. Four models used 9,015 plant-years in eastern and western US samples in 1965-1986 and 1987-2008. We controlled plant and year differences, winter warmth, winter sensitivity by latitude, and a latitude trend. Latitude interactions were +2.570, +0.874, +0.622 and +0.301 days per C per five degrees north. Only the early eastern interval was above zero after correction for four tests: +1.030 to +4.110. Adding a control for usual spring climate reduced that estimate to +0.892, with an interval of -1.230 to +3.014. A check on the same plants in both periods kept the one clear and three uncertain results. These data did not establish a clear common latitude relation separate from local climate. Different lilac types, changing site coverage, unknown visits, coarse seasonal weather, and few clusters limit inference. This is an ecological timing study. It does not test pollution, daily extremes, genetic adaptation, or a causal climate-change effect. The package includes the source recipe, measured hashes, selected panel, code, all results, numerical checks, and a figure.

display.caption: Left: latitude changes in spring bloom slopes in four main samples. Bars are 98.75% marginal intervals from summed state and year covariance. Right: estimates from sensitivity models, with no intervals. The same-plant check was added after the main fits. A positive value means a less negative spring slope farther north. East uses cloned lilac; West uses common lilac.

citations.reason: We reuse its unchanged raw-data builder for a new latitude interaction question. Source observations overlap; this is not independent evidence from that campaign publication.
Modern eastern US study reports stronger temperature sensitivity at lower latitude. Our historical lilac study tests the direction with a different model and records.
Defines the standard two-way covariance reported as a diagnostic. Our main intervals use the sum without the intersection subtraction, as stated before fitting.
